Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, the only time is the prescribed initial time and the solution map is the identity, so the claims hold. Otherwise lift $G$ periodically to $\widetilde G:J\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and write $z=(x,v)$ and $B(t,z)=(v,\widetilde G(t,x))$. On every compact time interval and bounded state ball, $B$ is continuous, bounded and Lipschitz in state because $D_xG$ is bounded. Thus [F1] gives unique local solutions. Along any such solution, if $M:=\sup_{I\times\mathbb T^d}|G|$, then $|V(t)-v_0|\le M|t-a|$ and $|X(t)-x_0-(t-a)v_0|\le M|t-a|^2/2$ for lifted positions. Hence a solution on a finite subinterval of $I$ remains in one bounded state cylinder. On a slightly larger cylinder the field has one finite bound and one finite state-Lipschitz constant, so the quantitative [F1] time estimate gives a common positive continuation length for every point of the trajectory. Finitely many such equal-length continuations cover $I$. Uniqueness on overlaps from [F1] gives one solution on all of $I$.

Fix a compact subinterval and a base state $z_0$. The bound on $D_zB$ and [F2] give $|z(t,z_0+h)-z(t,z_0)|\le C|h|$ uniformly in $t$ for small $h$. In the integral equations, set $\Delta_h(t):=z(t,z_0+h)-z(t,z_0)$ and $A_h(t):=\int_0^1D_zB\bigl(t,z(t,z_0)+\theta\Delta_h(t)\bigr)\,d\theta.$ Then $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_a^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds$. Uniform continuity of $D_zB$ on the compact time interval and torus gives $A_h\to A:=D_zB(t,z(t,z_0))$ uniformly in $t$. The linear integral equation $J(t)=I+\int_a^t A(s)J(s)\,ds$ has a unique solution by the same Picard iteration as [F1]. Subtracting it from the equation for $\Delta_h$, applying [F2], and using $\sup_t\|A_h-A\|\to0$ proves $\sup_t|\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h|/|h|\to0$. Thus $D_{z_0}z(t,z_0)=J(t)$ and it satisfies $\dot J=D_zB(t,z(t,z_0))J$, $J(a)=I$. Since $D_zB$ is bounded uniformly in state, [F2] also gives $\sup_{t\in I,z_0}\|J(t,z_0)\|<\infty$.

For each $r\ge2$, the candidate $r$-th state derivative $J_r$ satisfies the linear variational equation $\dot J_r=D_zB(t,z)J_r+\sum_{\substack{\pi\text{ a partition of }\{1,\ldots,r\}\\|\pi|\ge2}}D_z^{|\pi|}B(t,z)\bigl[J_{|C_1|},\ldots,J_{|C_{|\pi|}|}\bigr],\qquad J_r(a)=0,$ where $C_1,\ldots,C_{|\pi|}$ are the blocks of $\pi$ and $z=z(t,z_0)$. The coefficient and all higher derivatives of $B$ are bounded uniformly in state. By induction, the forcing term is therefore bounded uniformly over initial states; [F2] gives a unique $J_r$ with a uniform finite-time bound. Applying the difference-quotient argument of step 1.2 to the equation for $J_{r-1}$, using uniform continuity of each $D_z^jB$ on the compact time interval and periodic state variable for $j\le r$, shows that this $J_r$ is its derivative. Induction proves smooth dependence and the asserted uniform bounds. Solving the same system backward in time gives the inverse map, and uniqueness makes the two maps inverse. If $B$ is also smooth in time, $\partial_tz=B(t,z)$ and the state-jet equations give every mixed time-state derivative by repeated chain rule.

$$\theta_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d p_i^a\,dq_i^a,\qquad \omega_N:=-d\theta_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_i^a.$$

Overlaps of these position charts are translations by vectors in $L\mathbb Z^d$, with the same momentum coordinates, so $dq_i^a$ and $p_i^a$ agree on overlaps. $$H_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+\frac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}W(q_i-q_j).$$

The interaction force is $K(q):=-\nabla_qW(q)$, in newtons. It is bounded and globally Lipschitz on the compact torus; evenness of $W$ makes $K$ odd and $K(0)=0$. Hamilton's equations in the canonical convention are

$$\dot q_i=\frac{p_i}{m},\qquad \dot p_i=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}K(q_i-q_j).$$

For any chosen momentum scale $P_0>0$ in kilogram-metres per second, define the time scale $\tau_0:=mL/P_0$ in seconds, dimensionless variables $x_i:=q_i/L\in\mathbb T^d:=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$, $v_i:=p_i/P_0$, and $s:=t/\tau_0$. Define the dimensionless potential $\Phi(x):=mW(Lx)/P_0^2$ and force $k(x):=-\nabla_x\Phi(x)$. Then the equations become

$$x_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}k(x_i-x_j),$$

where prime denotes derivative with respect to dimensionless time $s$. Here
$\|Dk\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^d}\|Dk(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, with operator
norm induced by the Euclidean norm, and $\|k\|_\infty:=\sup_x|k(x)|$; the
constants $A:=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $B:=\|k\|_\infty$ are finite and
dimensionless. This is the selected smooth periodic mean-field scaling; it is
not the hard-sphere Boltzmann-Grad scaling.

Adopt $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the density-measure construction
([[def-countable-choice]]). A **Hamiltonian phase datum** consists of a
Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ of finite even dimension $2n$
without boundary, a symplectic form $\omega$ on $M$, and an autonomous smooth
function $H:M\to\mathbb R$. Here symplectic means that $\omega$ is a smooth
closed two-form and is nondegenerate at every point
([[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]). The Hamiltonian vector field
$X_H$ is the unique smooth field satisfying $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$
([[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]],
[[thm-hamiltonian-vector-fields-exist-uniquely-for-smooth-functions]]).
For each $z\in M$, let $I_z\subseteq\mathbb R$ be the maximal open interval
containing $0$ on which the unique maximal $C^\infty$ integral curve
$\gamma_z:I_z\to M$ satisfying $\dot\gamma_z(t)=X_H(\gamma_z(t))$ and
$\gamma_z(0)=z$ is defined; its existence and uniqueness follow from the
smooth ODE theorem ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-autonomous-smooth-odes]]).
Set $D=\{(t,z):z\in M,\ t\in I_z\}$ and define the maximal local flow
$\Phi:D\to M$ by $\Phi(t,z)=\gamma_z(t)$. Write $\Phi_t(z)=\Phi(t,z)$ when
$(t,z)\in D$. Uniqueness gives $\Phi_0(z)=z$ and
$\Phi_t(\Phi_s(z))=\Phi_{t+s}(z)$ whenever the terms are defined.
The domain $D$ is open, and in local charts $\Phi$ is smooth in the initial
state and $C^1$ in time, as supplied by the stated ODE theorem.
Completeness of the flow on all of $M$ is not part of this datum.

A Borel set $R\subseteq M$ is a **complete invariant domain** for this datum
if $\{t\}\times R\subseteq D$ and $\Phi_t(R)=R$ for every
$t\in\mathbb R$. Thus each restricted map $\Phi_t|_R:R\to R$ is defined
everywhere on $R$. The definition makes no assertion that $M$ itself is
complete or that such an $R$ has finite measure.

The symplectic orientation has volume form $\Omega=\omega^n/n!$
([[cor-symplectic-manifolds-have-a-canonical-orientation-and-volume-form]]).
For a fixed positive reference action $a_0$, define the positive smooth density
$\eta_0=|\Omega|/a_0^n$ and let $m_0$ be its intrinsic Borel measure
([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]],
[[def-borel-measurable-nonnegative-density-on-a-manifold]],
[[thm-density-measure-is-independent-of-the-chart-gluing]],
[[thm-a-positive-smooth-density-defines-a-locally-finite-radon-measure]]).
The measure $m_0$ may have infinite total mass. Use SI units for a physical
interpretation. In a standard mechanical cotangent chart, $q^i$ has unit m,
$p_i$ has unit kg m/s, $H$ has unit J, $\omega$ and $a_0$ have unit J s, and
$\eta_0$ is dimensionless. The scale $a_0$ is a normalization convention and
does not assert quantization.

An **ensemble** on $R$ is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $R$, distinct
from an individual trajectory. If $\mu$ has density $\rho$ with respect to
$m_0|_R$, then $\rho\ge0$ is Borel and $\int_R\rho\,dm_0=1$. For $\beta>0$,
the **canonical probability**, when it exists, is the Borel measure
$$\mu_\beta(B)=Z_\beta^{-1}\int_B e^{-\beta H}\,dm_0,\qquad Z_\beta=\int_R e^{-\beta H}\,dm_0,$$
for Borel $B\subseteq R$, provided $0<Z_\beta<\infty$. For a
temperature-parameterized physical interpretation, take $T>0$ as an absolute
temperature in K and $k_B>0$ as a supplied energy-temperature conversion
constant in J/K, and set $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

On a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, every Hamiltonian local flow

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Lift the torus positions periodically to $\mathbb R^{dN}$. The force bound $K_*:=\|K\|_\infty$ gives $|p_i(t)-p_i(0)|\le K_*|t|$ and $|q_i(t)-q_i(0)-(t/m)p_i(0)|\le K_*t^2/(2m)$ for each particle. Thus on every finite time interval the lifted trajectory stays in a bounded state cylinder. The lifted vector field from [F1] is smooth with bounded first derivatives there, so [F3] gives a common local continuation interval; repeating this fixed extension across the finite interval gives a global lifted solution, and periodicity makes it a well-defined torus solution. Reversing time gives existence on negative intervals. Local smooth dependence from [F3], composed over finitely many local intervals, makes every global finite-time map smooth; uniqueness makes $\Phi_{-t}^N$ its inverse.

With the symplectic form in [F1] and Hamiltonian sign convention in [F2], the Hamiltonian in [F1] defines the canonical Hamiltonian vector field on this cotangent phase space. Apply [F4] on each local time interval of step 1.1 and compose the volume-preserving local maps; this gives $(\Phi_t^N)^*\Omega_N=\Omega_N$ for every real $t$. The Hamiltonian vector field is equivariant under every permutation $\sigma$ of particle labels because the kinetic sum and even pair-potential sum are invariant. Hence $\sigma\Phi_t^N(z)$ and $\Phi_t^N(\sigma z)$ solve the same initial-value problem; uniqueness from [F3] gives equality.

Along characteristics $z(t)=\Phi_t^N(z_0)$, the derivative of $F_N(t,z(t))=F_N^0(z_0)$ is zero. The chain rule therefore gives $\partial_tF_N+X_{H_N}\cdot
abla F_N=0$. Substituting the Hamilton equations from [F1] and grouping the two terms for each pair $i<j$, using $K(q_j-q_i)=-K(q_i-q_j)$, yields $\partial_tF_N+\sum_{i=1}^N rac{p_i}{m}\cdot
abla_{q_i}F_N+ rac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}K(q_i-q_j)\cdot(
abla_{p_i}-
abla_{p_j})F_N=0.$ The rapid tails justify the displayed derivatives as classical ones on every finite time slab.

On each finite time slab the rapid bounds on all phase derivatives make $\partial_tF_N$ integrable and supply one integrable majorant for its time difference quotients; [F6] therefore permits differentiation under the $d\Omega_N$ integral. Integrate the equation in step 3.1 over all phase variables. The $q_i$-derivative terms have zero integral by periodicity. For each force term, $K(q_i-q_j)$ is independent of momenta, so integration by parts in $p_i$ and $p_j$ has zero boundary terms by the rapid tails. Fubini [F5] justifies these coordinate integrations and their order. Hence $\frac d{dt}\int F_N(t)\,d\Omega_N=0$; its value is $1$ at $t=0$ by [A2], so $F_N(t)$ remains normalized. The same permutation identity from step 2.1 and [A2] give $F_N(t,\sigma z)=F_N(t,z)$. Finally, the vector field derivatives of every order are bounded globally: its first derivative has entries $1/m$ and $DK$, and higher derivatives are bounded derivatives of the periodic force. The variational equations and [F3] bound every finite state derivative of $\Phi_{-t}^N$ on the time slab. Since $|p_i(t)-p_i(0)|\le K_*|t|$, the momentum norms differ by at most $\sqrt N K_*|t|$; the chain rule transfers every rapid-decay bound of $F_N^0$ to $F_N(t)$ uniformly on the slab.

and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $F:M\to N$ be a diffeomorphism of oriented smooth $n$-manifolds and
$\omega\in\Omega_c^n(N)$. If $F$ preserves orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=\int_N\omega$; if it reverses orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=-\int_N\omega$. If the sign varies between components,
apply the appropriate signed equality on each component and add. The
compact-support integrals are the choice-free finite-chart values, equal to
the global partition integrals whenever those are available.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Use $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ and
$d_Z((x,v),(y,w))=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)+|v-w|$ from
[[def-csm-dk-phase-space-wasserstein-one]]. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $Z$. If

$$\int_Z\varphi\,d\mu=\int_Z\varphi\,d\nu \quad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Z),$$

where $C_c^\infty(Z)$ means smooth and periodic in position with compact
velocity support, then $\mu=\nu$ on all Borel subsets of $Z$.

Use the dimensionless one-particle phase space $Z:=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ from [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]], with its product topology and Borel sigma algebra. The finite torus is second-countable by [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]], and Euclidean space is second-countable. Consequently $Z$ and $Z\times Z$ are second-countable, and the Borel sigma algebra of each finite product equals the product of the factor Borel sigma algebras: every open set is a countable union of basic open rectangles. Use the product topology and its Borel sigma algebra on $Z\times Z$ as well.

For $x,y\in\mathbb T^d$, let

$$d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y):=\min_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^d}|\widetilde x-\widetilde y+\ell|,$$

where $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in\mathbb R^d$ are any representatives; the minimum is independent of the representatives. Equip $Z$ with

$$d_Z((x,v),(y,w)):=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)+|v-w|.$$

Let $\mathcal P_1(Z)$ be the Borel probability measures $\mu$ on $Z$ with $\int_Z|v|\,d\mu(x,v)<\infty$. For $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, a coupling is a Borel probability $\pi$ on $Z\times Z$ satisfying $\pi(A\times Z)=\mu(A)$ and $\pi(Z\times B)=\nu(B)$ for all Borel $A,B\subseteq Z$; write $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ for the set of couplings. Define the phase-space Wasserstein-1 coupling cost by

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{Z\times Z}d_Z(z,z')\,d\pi(z,z').$$

By [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], $\mu\otimes\nu$ is a probability on $\mathcal B(Z)\otimes\mathcal B(Z)=\mathcal B(Z\times Z)$ and its marginals are $\mu,\nu$; hence $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is nonempty. The infimum is finite: this product coupling has torus cost at most $\sqrt d/2$, and Tonelli's theorem bounds its velocity cost by $\int|v|\,d\mu+\int|w|\,d\nu$. No minimizing coupling is assumed to exist.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: Choose $h>0$ with $Ah^2<1$; when $A=0$ any finite $h$ is allowed. For a bounded continuous displacement $u(s,x,v)$ in $\mathbb R^d$ on $[0,h]\times Z$, periodic in $x$ and with $u(0,\cdot)=0$, set $(Tu)(s,x,v):=\int_0^s(s-r)\int_Z k\bigl(x+rv+u(r,x,v)-y-rw-u(r,y,w)\bigr)\,d\mu_0(y,w)\,dr.$ with torus arguments understood modulo $\mathbb Z^d$. On the closed set $\sup|u|\le Bh^2/2$, the map has the same bound because $|k|\le B$. For every convergent sequence of $(s,x,v)$, the integrand is pointwise continuous in those variables and bounded by $B$ on $(Z,\mathcal B(Z),\mu_0)$; [F3] therefore gives joint continuity of $Tu$. Uniform limits preserve continuity, periodicity and the initial condition, so this closed function space is complete in the supremum norm.

For any two displacements $u,\widetilde u$, the force arguments change by at most $2\sup|u-\widetilde u|$. The Lipschitz bound $A$ and $\int_0^s(s-r)\,dr=s^2/2$ give $\sup|Tu-T\widetilde u|\le Ah^2\sup|u-\widetilde u|$. Starting with $u_0=0$ and iterating $u_{n+1}=Tu_n$, successive differences are bounded by a geometric sequence with ratio $Ah^2<1$; hence $(u_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $u$ belongs to the closed complete set, and the Lipschitz estimate gives $Tu=u$. The same estimate makes this fixed point unique.

Put $X_s(x,v)=x+sv+u(s,x,v)$ modulo the torus and $V_s(x,v)=v+\partial_su(s,x,v)$. The Volterra formula and continuity of the integrand imply $\partial_s^2X_s=\int_Zk(X_s(x,v)-X_s(y,w))\,d\mu_0(y,w)$, with $X_0=x$ and $\dot X_0=v$; thus $(X_s,V_s)$ solves the displayed characteristic system. The bound $|V_s-v|\le B|s|$ gives a finite first moment for every finite $s$. For bounded continuous $\psi$, the integrand $\psi(X_s,V_s)$ is pointwise continuous in $s$ and bounded by $\|\psi\|_\infty$, so [F3] gives narrow continuity of $\mu_s$.

The force $F_{\mu_s}(x)$ is continuous in $(s,x)$: for $(s_n,x_n)\to(s,x)$, its integrand converges pointwise and is bounded by $B$, so [F3] applies on $(Z,\mu_0)$. Along each characteristic, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{ds}\varphi(s,X_s,V_s) =\bigl(\partial_s\varphi+V_s\cdot\nabla_x\varphi +F_{\mu_s}(X_s)\cdot\nabla_v\varphi\bigr)(s,X_s,V_s).$ On any bounded time interval the right side is bounded by $C(1+|v|)$, which is integrable by the assumed first moment. Difference quotients have the same common bound; [F3] therefore permits differentiation under the $\mu_0$ integral and gives exactly the weak identity in the Statement.

The fixed-point estimate and force bounds do not depend on the starting time or probability. Repeating the construction on successive intervals of length $h$ therefore gives a unique characteristic solution on every bounded positive interval. For negative times let $R(x,v)=(x,-v)$ and solve the same positive-time problem from $R_\#\mu_0$. If its characteristics are $(\widetilde X_r,\widetilde V_r)$, define, for $s\le0$, $X_s(x,v)=\widetilde X_{-s}(x,-v)$ and $V_s(x,v)=-\widetilde V_{-s}(x,-v)$. Then $X_0=x$, $V_0=v$, $\dot X_s=V_s$, and $\dot V_s=F_{\mu_s}(X_s)$: the transformed law has the same position marginal as $\mu_s$, and the force depends only on position. Thus these are characteristics from $\mu_0$ for negative times. Uniqueness on overlapping intervals follows from step 2.1 and continuation, so the positive and negative solutions form one global family.

Suppose $\mu_0$ has the smooth density and all moments in the Statement. Its characteristic field is $b(s,x,v)=(v,F_{\mu_s}(x))$. Every state derivative of $F_{\mu_s}$ is bounded on a finite time slab because it is an integral of a bounded derivative of $k$. Step 4.1 makes $b$ continuous in time; [F2] gives a smooth state flow $S_{s,0}$ and its smooth backward inverse. Its state derivative $J_s=D S_{s,0}$ solves $\dot J_s=D b(s,S_{s,0})J_s$, $J_0=I$, by [F2]. The divergence of $b$ is zero: $\nabla_x\cdot v=0$ and $F_{\mu_s}$ is independent of $v$. Since the inverse flow makes $J_s$ invertible, multilinear differentiation of its determinant gives $\frac d{ds}\det J_s=\det J_s\,\operatorname{tr}(J_s^{-1}D b\,J_s) =\det J_s\,\operatorname{tr}(D b)=0$; with $\det J_0=1$ this yields $\det J_s=1$. Define $\rho_s=\rho_0\circ S_{0,s}$ relative to $dx\,dv$. It is smooth in state, and the chain rule gives the classical transport equation.

Orient $Z$ by its standard translation-chart volume form $\mathrm{vol}=dx^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^d\wedge dv^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv^d$. By [F9] and [F10], its associated volume measure is the product $dx\,dv$ specified in the statement. Since $\det J_s=1$, $S_{s,0}$ preserves this orientation. For $g\in C_c^\infty(Z)$ the top form $g\rho_s\,\mathrm{vol}$ has compact support, so [F4] and step 5.1 give $\int_Zg(z)\rho_s(z)\,dx\,dv =\int_Zg(S_{s,0}z)\rho_s(S_{s,0}z)\,dx\,dv =\int_Zg(S_{s,0}z)\rho_0(z)\,dx\,dv.$ Take the cutoffs $\chi_R(v)$ of [F5] for positive integers $R$. The identity with $g=\chi_R$ gives $\int_{|v|\le R}\rho_s\,dx\,dv\le\int_Z\chi_R\rho_s\,dx\,dv=\int_Z\chi_R(V_s(z))\rho_0(z)\,dx\,dv\le1$, since $\rho_s\ge0$ and $0\le\chi_R\le1$. The indicators of the balls $\{|v|\le R\}$ increase to $1$, so [F6] implies $\int_Z\rho_s\,dx\,dv\le1$. Now $\rho_s$ is integrable and $\chi_R(v)\to1$ pointwise. Apply [F3] to both sides of the cutoff identity, with majorants $\rho_s$ and $\rho_0$, to obtain $\int_Z\rho_s\,dx\,dv=\int_Z\rho_0\,dx\,dv=1$. Thus $\rho_s\,dx\,dv$ is a probability. The identity also says $\rho_s\,dx\,dv$ and the characteristic law $\mu_s$ agree on all smooth compactly supported tests. Apply [F7] to conclude $\rho_s\,dx\,dv=\mu_s$, so $\rho_s$ is the density of $\mu_s$.

For every time-derivative order $r$, differentiating $F_{\mu_s}(x)=\int k(x-X_s(z))\rho_0(z)\,dz$ gives finite sums of bounded derivatives of $k$ times products of characteristic time derivatives. The base bounds $|V_s-v|\le B|s|$ and $|\dot V_s|\le B$, followed by induction in the differentiated characteristic equation, bound each order-$r$ integrand by $C(r,T)(1+|v|^r)$ on $|s|\le T$. Every such envelope is integrable by the all-moment assumption. Dominated convergence [F3] therefore justifies each time differentiation under the integral, so $F_{\mu_s}$ is jointly smooth in $(s,x)$. The joint-smooth-time clause of [F2] then makes $S_{s,0}$ and $\rho_s$ jointly smooth, proving the classical branch.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a side length $L>0$ in metres, a mass $m>0$ in kilograms, and a smooth even periodic pair potential $W\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R)$ in joules, where $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ is the flat position torus and even means $W(-q)=W(q)$. For each finite integer $N\ge1$, the phase space is $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ with canonical coordinates $z_i=(q_i,p_i)$, $q_i\in\mathbb T_L^d$ in metres and $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ in kilogram-metres per second. In position charts obtained by lifting torus coordinates to $\mathbb R^d$, define

$$\theta_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d p_i^a\,dq_i^a,\qquad \omega_N:=-d\theta_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_i^a.$$

Overlaps of these position charts are translations by vectors in $L\mathbb Z^d$, with the same momentum coordinates, so $dq_i^a$ and $p_i^a$ agree on overlaps. Thus the displayed forms glue globally on $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$; $\omega_N$ is closed and nondegenerate by its displayed coordinate matrix. Both forms have action units of joule-seconds. Use the Hamiltonian convention $\iota_{X_{H_N}}\omega_N=dH_N$ of [[def-csm-dk-hamiltonian-flow-measure]]. The finite-particle Hamiltonian, with energy in joules, is

$$H_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+\frac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}W(q_i-q_j).$$

The interaction force is $K(q):=-\nabla_qW(q)$, in newtons. It is bounded and globally Lipschitz on the compact torus; evenness of $W$ makes $K$ odd and $K(0)=0$. Hamilton's equations in the canonical convention are

$$\dot q_i=\frac{p_i}{m},\qquad \dot p_i=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}K(q_i-q_j).$$

For any chosen momentum scale $P_0>0$ in kilogram-metres per second, define the time scale $\tau_0:=mL/P_0$ in seconds, dimensionless variables $x_i:=q_i/L\in\mathbb T^d:=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$, $v_i:=p_i/P_0$, and $s:=t/\tau_0$. Define the dimensionless potential $\Phi(x):=mW(Lx)/P_0^2$ and force $k(x):=-\nabla_x\Phi(x)$. Then the equations become

$$x_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}k(x_i-x_j),$$

where prime denotes derivative with respect to dimensionless time $s$. Here

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{Z\times Z}d_Z(z,z')\,d\pi(z,z').$$

spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Use $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ and
$d_Z((x,v),(y,w))=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)+|v-w|$ from
[[def-csm-dk-phase-space-wasserstein-one]]. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $Z$. If

$$\int_Z\varphi\,d\mu=\int_Z\varphi\,d\nu \quad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Z),$$

where $C_c^\infty(Z)$ means smooth and periodic in position with compact
velocity support, then $\mu=\nu$ on all Borel subsets of $Z$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Fix a coupling $\pi_0$ of $\mu_0$ and $
u_0$. Write the two characteristics as $(X_s,V_s)$ and $(Y_s,W_s)$, and push $\pi_0$ forward by their product flow to obtain $\pi_s$. Define $D_x(s)=\int d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s,Y_s)\,d\pi_0$, $D_v(s)=\int|V_s-W_s|\,d\pi_0$, and $D=D_x+D_v$. The torus distance along absolutely continuous curves has upper derivative at most $|V_s-W_s|$. For an outer pair $(z,w)$, write $F_{\mu_s}(X_s(z))=\int k(X_s(z)-X_s(z'))\,d\pi_0(z',w')$ and $F_{
u_s}(Y_s(w))=\int k(Y_s(w)-Y_s(w'))\,d\pi_0(z',w')$, using the two marginals of $\pi_0$. The torus triangle inequality and the $A$-Lipschitz bound for $k$ give a force difference at most $A(d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s(z),Y_s(w))+d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s(z'),Y_s(w')))$. Integrating the inner pair $(z',w')$ against $\pi_0$ bounds this by $A(d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s(z),Y_s(w))+D_x(s))$. On every bounded time slab the velocity difference is bounded by its integrable initial difference plus $2\|k\|_\infty |s|$, and the acceleration difference is at most $2\|k\|_\infty$. Integrate the pathwise distance inequalities in time and against the outer $\pi_0$; Tonelli [F6] justifies the order of integration and gives $D(s)\le D(0)+\int_0^s(D_v(r)+2A D_x(r))\,dr\le D(0)+(1+2A)\int_0^sD(r)\,dr$. Gronwall [F9] gives $D(s)\le e^{(1+2A)s}D(0)$. For negative time, the transformation $R(x,v)=(x,-v)$ sends a solution run backward to a forward solution starting from $R_\#\mu_0$ (and likewise for $
u_0$). Explicitly, if the original characteristic starts at $(x,v)$ with law $\mu_0$, set $\widetilde X_r=X_{-r}(x,v)$ and $\widetilde V_r=-V_{-r}(x,v)$; the reversed initial state is $(x,-v)$. Then $\dot{\widetilde X}=\widetilde V$ and $\dot{\widetilde V}=F_{\mu_{-r}}(\widetilde X)=F_{R_\#\mu_{-r}}(\widetilde X)$, because the force depends only on position. Thus $R_\#\mu_{-r}$ is a forward solution starting at $R_\#\mu_0$. Since $R$ preserves $d_Z$, the positive-time estimate for these reversed solutions proves the estimate with $|s|$.

Let $\sigma_s$ be a weak solution in the Statement and set $F_s(x)=\int k(x-y)\,d\sigma_s(y,w)$. Narrow continuity and boundedness of $k$ make $F_s(x)$ continuous in $(s,x)$; every state derivative is bounded by the corresponding bound on $k$. By [F5] the field $(v,F_s(x))$ has a complete state flow on every bounded time interval and bounded state derivatives of that flow there. For fixed terminal $t$ and $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Z)$, compose $\psi$ with the characteristic map from time $s$ to $t$. Bounded acceleration makes the preimage of its compact velocity support remain in a bounded velocity set on the finite slab, so the resulting time-dependent test $\phi(s,z)$, its first state derivatives, and its time derivative are bounded. It satisfies $\partial_s\phi+v\cdot\nabla_x\phi+F_s\cdot\nabla_v\phi=0$. The weak identity makes $\int\phi(s,z)\,d\sigma_s(z)$ constant, hence $\int\psi\,d\sigma_t=\int\psi(S_{t,0}(z))\,d\sigma_0(z)$. This is equality on every smooth compactly supported test, so the phase-space measure lemma [F8] gives $\sigma_t=(S_{t,0})_\#\sigma_0$.

The measure $\pi_s$ is a coupling of $\mu_s$ and $\nu_s$, so [F2] gives $\mathcal W_1(\mu_s,\nu_s)\le D(s)$. The estimate in step 1.1 holds for every coupling $\pi_0$; taking the infimum of its right side gives the first claimed inequality without assuming an optimal coupling exists.

The trajectory defined in the Statement is complete by [F3]. Differentiating its coordinate and time rescaling using [F1] shows that $Z_i(s)=(X_i(s),V_i(s))$ satisfies $\dot X_i=V_i$ and $\dot V_i=N^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}k(X_i-X_j)$. Since $k(0)=0$, this equals $N^{-1}\sum_jk(X_i-X_j)$, the characteristic force generated by $\mu_N(s)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{Z_i(s)}$. The coordinatewise map $\Xi_N$ commutes with label permutations, so the conjugated flow retains the permutation equivariance in [F3]. The finite sum $F_{\mu_N(s)}$ is continuous in time, smooth in position and bounded with all state derivatives; [F5] therefore supplies its characteristic flow for every initial state. ODE uniqueness identifies this flow at each initial atom with the particle trajectory, so its push-forward of $\mu_N(0)$ is $\mu_N(s)$. The initial empirical law is in $\mathcal P_1(Z)$, and uniqueness of the global characteristic evolution in [F4] identifies $\mu_N(s)$ with that evolution from $\mu_N(0)$. Applying step 2.1 to initial laws $\mu_N(0)$ and $\mu_0$ gives the particle estimate.

By step 1.2 any two weak solutions with the same initial law are the characteristic evolutions of that law. Step 2.1 gives zero $\mathcal W_1$ between them at each time; alternatively their representation in step 1.2 already identifies both with the same push-forward. This proves uniqueness in the stated weak class.

abla_{p_j}F_N$ integrates to zero because $K(q_i-q_j)$ is independent of $p_j$ and the $p_j$-tail vanishes at infinity. The term containing $
abla_{p_i}F_N$ remains. By permutation symmetry of $F_N$, for fixed $i\le k$ every label $j>k$ has the same integrated contribution, equal to $
abla_{p_i}\cdot\int K(q_i-q_{k+1})f_{k+1}(t,z_1,\ldots,z_k,z_{k+1})\,dz_{k+1}.$ There are exactly $N-k$ such labels, each carrying coefficient $1/N$. This gives the factor $(N-k)/N$ and all terms of the displayed hierarchy.

If $k=N$, there are no cross pairs, so the same integration argument leaves only the one-body transport and internal-pair terms; the formula's cross coefficient is $(N-N)/N=0$. Thus the statement holds for every $1\le k\le N$, with no factorization assumption at any step.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a side length $L>0$ in metres, a mass $m>0$ in kilograms, and a smooth even periodic pair potential $W\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R)$ in joules, where $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ is the flat position torus and even means $W(-q)=W(q)$. For each finite integer $N\ge1$, the phase space is $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ with canonical coordinates $z_i=(q_i,p_i)$, $q_i\in\mathbb T_L^d$ in metres and $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ in kilogram-metres per second. In position charts obtained by lifting torus coordinates to $\mathbb R^d$, define

$$\theta_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d p_i^a\,dq_i^a,\qquad \omega_N:=-d\theta_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_i^a.$$

Overlaps of these position charts are translations by vectors in $L\mathbb Z^d$, with the same momentum coordinates, so $dq_i^a$ and $p_i^a$ agree on overlaps. Thus the displayed forms glue globally on $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$; $\omega_N$ is closed and nondegenerate by its displayed coordinate matrix. Both forms have action units of joule-seconds. Use the Hamiltonian convention $\iota_{X_{H_N}}\omega_N=dH_N$ of [[def-csm-dk-hamiltonian-flow-measure]]. The finite-particle Hamiltonian, with energy in joules, is

$$H_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+\frac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}W(q_i-q_j).$$

The interaction force is $K(q):=-\nabla_qW(q)$, in newtons. It is bounded and globally Lipschitz on the compact torus; evenness of $W$ makes $K$ odd and $K(0)=0$. Hamilton's equations in the canonical convention are

$$\dot q_i=\frac{p_i}{m},\qquad \dot p_i=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}K(q_i-q_j).$$

For any chosen momentum scale $P_0>0$ in kilogram-metres per second, define the time scale $\tau_0:=mL/P_0$ in seconds, dimensionless variables $x_i:=q_i/L\in\mathbb T^d:=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$, $v_i:=p_i/P_0$, and $s:=t/\tau_0$. Define the dimensionless potential $\Phi(x):=mW(Lx)/P_0^2$ and force $k(x):=-\nabla_x\Phi(x)$. Then the equations become

$$x_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}k(x_i-x_j),$$

where prime denotes derivative with respect to dimensionless time $s$. Here
$\|Dk\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^d}\|Dk(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, with operator
norm induced by the Euclidean norm, and $\|k\|_\infty:=\sup_x|k(x)|$; the
constants $A:=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $B:=\|k\|_\infty$ are finite and
dimensionless. This is the selected smooth periodic mean-field scaling; it is
not the hard-sphere Boltzmann-Grad scaling.

Use the dimensionless one-particle phase space $Z:=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ from [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]], with its product topology and Borel sigma algebra. The finite torus is second-countable by [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]], and Euclidean space is second-countable. Consequently $Z$ and $Z\times Z$ are second-countable, and the Borel sigma algebra of each finite product equals the product of the factor Borel sigma algebras: every open set is a countable union of basic open rectangles. Use the product topology and its Borel sigma algebra on $Z\times Z$ as well.

For $x,y\in\mathbb T^d$, let

$$d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y):=\min_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^d}|\widetilde x-\widetilde y+\ell|,$$

where $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in\mathbb R^d$ are any representatives; the minimum is independent of the representatives. Equip $Z$ with

$$d_Z((x,v),(y,w)):=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)+|v-w|.$$

Let $\mathcal P_1(Z)$ be the Borel probability measures $\mu$ on $Z$ with $\int_Z|v|\,d\mu(x,v)<\infty$. For $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, a coupling is a Borel probability $\pi$ on $Z\times Z$ satisfying $\pi(A\times Z)=\mu(A)$ and $\pi(Z\times B)=\nu(B)$ for all Borel $A,B\subseteq Z$; write $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ for the set of couplings. Define the phase-space Wasserstein-1 coupling cost by

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{Z\times Z}d_Z(z,z')\,d\pi(z,z').$$

By [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], $\mu\otimes\nu$ is a probability on $\mathcal B(Z)\otimes\mathcal B(Z)=\mathcal B(Z\times Z)$ and its marginals are $\mu,\nu$; hence $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is nonempty. The infimum is finite: this product coupling has torus cost at most $\sqrt d/2$, and Tonelli's theorem bounds its velocity cost by $\int|v|\,d\mu+\int|w|\,d\nu$. No minimizing coupling is assumed to exist.

Assume countable choice [[def-countable-choice]] for the intrinsic
density-measure construction in [[def-csm-dk-hamiltonian-flow-measure]]. On
$(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$, use the canonical form
$\omega_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_{i,a}$ and Liouville
volume form $\Omega_N:=\omega_N^{dN}/(dN)!$. The positive reference density
$|\Omega_N|/a_0^{dN}$ induces a Borel measure $m_{0,N}$ by that definition;
write $d\Omega_N:=a_0^{dN}dm_{0,N}$ for canonical Liouville measure, which
in canonical coordinates is $dq_1\,dp_1\cdots dq_N\,dp_N$. Fix $d\ge1$,
$m,L>0$, a finite integer $N\ge1$, and the periodic smooth even potential
and canonical phase-space convention of
[[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. The associated Hamiltonian ODE has
a unique complete smooth flow $\Phi_t^N$ on $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ for all
$t\in\mathbb R$. It preserves $\Omega_N$ and commutes with permutations of
the $N$ particle labels.

If the initial law has a normalized symmetric $C^\infty$ density
$F_N^0(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$ relative to $d\Omega_N$ and, for
every pair of multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ and integer $r\ge0$,

$$\sup_{q\in(\mathbb T_L^d)^N,\ p\in\mathbb R^{dN}}(1+|p|)^r|\partial_q^\alpha\partial_p^\beta F_N^0(q,p)|<\infty,$$

then $F_N(t):=F_N^0\circ\Phi_{-t}^N$ is a normalized symmetric classical solution of the Liouville equation for all $t$. Its momentum tails, together with every phase derivative, remain rapidly decreasing uniformly on each bounded time interval.

Use $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$, $d_Z$, $\mathcal P_1(Z)$ and
$\mathcal W_1$ from [[def-csm-dk-phase-space-wasserstein-one]], and the odd
smooth force $k$ with $A=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $k(0)=0$ from
[[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. If $\mu_0,\nu_0\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$,
let $\mu_s,\nu_s$ be their global characteristic evolutions from
[[thm-csm-dk-global-lipschitz-vlasov]]. Then for every $s\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu_s,\nu_s)\le e^{(1+2A)|s|}\mathcal W_1(\mu_0,\nu_0).$$

For a finite integer $N\ge1$, choose the momentum scale $P_0>0$ and set
$\tau_0=mL/P_0$ as in [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. Define
$\Xi_N:Z^N\to(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ by
$\Xi_N((x_i,v_i)_{i=1}^N)=((Lx_i,P_0v_i)_{i=1}^N)$, where multiplication
by $L$ maps $\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ to $\mathbb R^d/L\mathbb Z^d$.
Write $\Phi_t^N$ for the complete flow in physical coordinates and time from
[[thm-csm-dk-finite-n-complete-flow]]. For initial points
$Z_1^0,\ldots,Z_N^0\in Z$, define their dimensionless trajectory by

$$ (Z_i(s))_{i=1}^N:=\Xi_N^{-1}\!\left(\Phi_{\tau_0s}^N\bigl(\Xi_N((Z_i^0)_{i=1}^N)\bigr)\right). $$

Put $\mu_N(s)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Z_i(s)}$. If $\mu_s$ is the characteristic
evolution from any $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, then

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(s),\mu_s)\le e^{(1+2A)|s|}\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0).$$

Finally, a narrowly continuous curve (meaning that $s\mapsto\int g\,d\sigma_s$
is continuous for every bounded continuous $g$) $\sigma_s\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$ with
locally bounded first velocity moments that satisfies the weak Vlasov identity
in [[thm-csm-dk-global-lipschitz-vlasov]] is the characteristic evolution from
its initial law. Thus this weak-solution class is unique. The estimate is for
the periodic second-order phase metric above; it is not Golse's first-order
estimate and does not use a collision or Boltzmann-Grad scaling.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: For any fixed $\nu\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, the map $z\mapsto\mathcal W_1(N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{z_i},\nu)$ is continuous. Indeed, split a coupling's mass at each repeated atom equally among its labels, and then move label $i$ from $z_i$ to $z_i'$ while keeping its target. The cost increases by at most $N^{-1}\sum_i d_Z(z_i,z_i')$. Taking infima and reversing the roles gives the same bound for the absolute difference of the two Wasserstein values. Thus the initial Wasserstein error is a measurable random variable, bounded by $D_K$ on $K^N$. For a finite Borel partition $\mathcal P=\{C_1,\ldots,C_M\}$ of $K$ with cell diameters at most $\delta$, put $p_j=\mu_0(C_j)$ and $P_{N,j}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1_{C_j}(Z_i(0))$. A coupling matches the common mass $\min(p_j,P_{N,j})$ inside each cell at cost at most $\delta$; the leftover mass is $r=\tfrac12\sum_j|P_{N,j}-p_j|$ and can be coupled across $K$ at cost at most $D_Kr$. Product measures in [F6] construct these within-cell and residual couplings (if $r=0$, no residual coupling is needed). Hence $\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0)\le\delta+(D_K/2)\sum_j|P_{N,j}-p_j|$. Independence [F1] gives $\mathbb E|P_{N,j}-p_j|^2=p_j(1-p_j)/N$, so [F7] gives $\mathbb E|P_{N,j}-p_j|\le\sqrt{p_j/N}$; therefore the sum of expected discrepancies is at most $\sqrt{M/N}$. Partition a bounded velocity box containing $K$ and the position torus into rectangular cells of side at most a fixed multiple of $\delta$; intersect with $K$ and disjointize the cover. There are at most $C_K\delta^{-2d}$ cells, each with $d_Z$-diameter at most $\delta$. This proves the expected initial bound in the Statement.

For each $\mu_0$, take every coordinate space to be $(Z,\mathcal B(Z))$ and set every history-dependent kernel to $K_n(z_0,\ldots,z_n,A)=\mu_0(A)$. For each fixed $A$ this is constant, hence measurable, and it is a probability measure in $A$. The Ionescu--Tulcea theorem [F2], under full Choice, supplies a probability on the countable product whose finite-prefix laws are the iterated products of $\mu_0$. Reindexing coordinates from 0 to 1 gives the sequence in the Statement; its common marginals and product finite-prefix laws make its coordinates mutually independent and identically distributed by [F1].

For a centered Bernoulli variable $Y=\mathbf1_{C_j}(Z_i)-p_j$, $\mathbb EY^2=p_j(1-p_j)$ and $\mathbb EY^4\le p_j$. Expanding the fourth power of the sum of independent centered variables leaves only terms with four equal indices or two equal pairs, so $\mathbb E|P_{N,j}-p_j|^4 =N^{-4}\left(N\mathbb EY^4+3N(N-1)(\mathbb EY^2)^2\right)\le4N^{-2}.$ For every rational $\varepsilon>0$, the elementary bound $\mathbb P(|P_{N,j}-p_j|>\varepsilon)\le \varepsilon^{-4}\mathbb E|P_{N,j}-p_j|^4$ makes $\sum_N\mathbb P(|P_{N,j}-p_j|>\varepsilon)<\infty$. By countable subadditivity, the probability of such deviations occurring for some $N\ge n$ is bounded by the tail of that convergent series, which tends to zero; hence for this rational $\varepsilon$ the deviations occur only finitely often almost surely. Intersect over rational $\varepsilon>0$, over the finitely many cells of each of a countable sequence of partitions with mesh $\delta_\ell\downarrow0$. The coupling bound in step 1.1 then gives $\limsup_N\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0)\le\delta_\ell$ for every $\ell$, so the initial Wasserstein distance tends to zero almost surely.

Step 1.1 and $M_\delta\le C_K\delta^{-2d}$ give $\mathbb E\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0)\le \delta+(D_K\sqrt{C_K}/2)\delta^{-d}N^{-1/2}$. Taking $\delta=N^{-1/(2d+2)}$ bounds both terms by constants times that power of $N$. Step 2.1 gives almost-sure convergence. To identify the trajectories used by [F4] and [F5], let $\Xi_N:Z^N\to(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ be $\Xi_N((x_i,v_i)_{i=1}^N)=((Lx_i\bmod L,P_0v_i)_{i=1}^N)$ and set $\tau_0=mL/P_0$, $k(x)=(mL/P_0^2)K(Lx)$ as in [F3]. For the first $N$ iid initial coordinates, define $(Z_i(s))_{i=1}^N:=\Xi_N^{-1}\!\left(\Phi_{\tau_0s}^N\bigl(\Xi_N((Z_i(0))_{i=1}^N)\bigr)\right)=\left(\left(q_i(\tau_0s)/L,p_i(\tau_0s)/P_0\right)\right)_{i=1}^N$, where $\Phi_t^N$ is the physical flow from [F4]. This is its conjugate in the dimensionless coordinates $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ and time $s$; differentiating and using the model equations gives $\dot X_i=V_i$ and $\dot V_i=N^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}k(X_i-X_j)$. Since $k(0)=0$, $\mu_N(s)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{Z_i(s)}$ is the empirical characteristic evolution to which [F5] applies. The coordinate scaling commutes with particle permutations, so the exchangeability used below follows from [F4] and the iid initial law. On $[-T,T]$ the particle trajectories depend continuously on time and their initial vector by [F4]. The characteristics carrying $\mu_0$ have uniformly bounded velocities there because $K$ is compact and $k$ is bounded. For two times $s,t$, transport the target of any empirical-to-$\mu_s$ coupling by the characteristic map from $s$ to $t$, and move its labelled source atoms from $Z_i(s)$ to $Z_i(t)$. The cost changes by at most $N^{-1}\sum_i d_Z(Z_i(s),Z_i(t))+\int d_Z(\chi_s z,\chi_t z)\,d\mu_0(z)$, which tends to zero as $t\to s$; reversing times proves continuity of the error. At each fixed time its dependence on the initial vector is continuous by the labelled-coupling bound above and [F4]. Its supremum over $[-T,T]$ therefore equals the supremum over a countable dense set of times and is measurable. Applying [F5] at every $|s|\le T$ yields the supremum bound with factor $e^{CT}$, both in expectation and almost surely.

The joint law of the finite particle vector is permutation invariant by [F4] and iid symmetry [F1]. Given the finite-particle configuration at time $s$, draw $k$ indices independently and uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. The resulting tuple has conditional law $\mu_N(s)^{\otimes k}$. The chance of an index collision is at most $\binom{k}{2}/N$ by a union bound. After averaging over the exchangeable particle vector, conditioning the index sampling on no collision makes the tuple's law equal to that of the first $k$ particles. Thus the expectation of $\Psi$ under the true $k$-law and under $\mu_N(s)^{\otimes k}$ differs by at most $2\|\Psi\|_\infty\binom{k}{2}/N$. For any coupling $\pi$ of $\mu_N(s)$ and $\mu_s$, its $k$-fold product from [F6] couples their product laws, and the sum-metric Lipschitz bound gives a test-integral difference at most $k\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)\int d_Z\,d\pi$. Taking the infimum over $\pi$, then expectation, and using [F5] gives the second term in the displayed bound. The estimate tends to zero uniformly for $|s|\le T$, establishing fixed-$k$ propagation of chaos in the stated test class.

citations.quote:
Adopt [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]] as the selected finite-particle model: for each $N\ge1$, the phase points $(q_i,p_i)$ evolve by its displayed Hamilton equations with smooth even periodic potential $W$ and interaction coefficient $1/N$. This is a model assumption with $q_i$ in metres, $p_i$ in kilogram-metres per second, $m$ in kilograms, $W$ in joules, and force $K=-\nabla W$ in newtons.

For the propagation-of-chaos preparation branch, give $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ its product topology and the Borel sigma algebra generated by its open sets. Choose a Borel probability $\mu_0$ and a compact set $K\subset Z$ with $\mu_0(K)=1$. Put $\Omega=Z^{\mathbb N}$ with product sigma algebra $\mathcal B(Z)^{\otimes\mathbb N}$. Under the full Axiom of Choice, [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] applied to the constant kernels $K_n(z_0,\ldots,z_n,A)=\mu_0(A)$ supplies a probability $P$ on $\Omega$. Let $Z_i(0):\Omega\to Z$ be the coordinate projections, and use the first $N$ coordinates for the finite-$N$ preparation. For every finite list of indices $i_1<\cdots<i_r$ and Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq Z$, this construction gives

$$P\bigl(Z_{i_1}(0)\in A_1,\ldots,Z_{i_r}(0)\in A_r\bigr)=\prod_{j=1}^r\mu_0(A_j).$$

Thus each coordinate has law $\mu_0$ and the coordinates are mutually independent. Here “iid” means exactly this common-marginal and finite-rectangle factorization property. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a side length $L>0$ in metres, a mass $m>0$ in kilograms, and a smooth even periodic pair potential $W\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R)$ in joules, where $\mathbb T_L^d:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ is the flat position torus and even means $W(-q)=W(q)$. For each finite integer $N\ge1$, the phase space is $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ with canonical coordinates $z_i=(q_i,p_i)$, $q_i\in\mathbb T_L^d$ in metres and $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ in kilogram-metres per second. In position charts obtained by lifting torus coordinates to $\mathbb R^d$, define

$$\theta_N:=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d p_i^a\,dq_i^a,\qquad \omega_N:=-d\theta_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{a=1}^d dq_i^a\wedge dp_i^a.$$

Overlaps of these position charts are translations by vectors in $L\mathbb Z^d$, with the same momentum coordinates, so $dq_i^a$ and $p_i^a$ agree on overlaps. Thus the displayed forms glue globally on $(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$; $\omega_N$ is closed and nondegenerate by its displayed coordinate matrix. Both forms have action units of joule-seconds. Use the Hamiltonian convention $\iota_{X_{H_N}}\omega_N=dH_N$ of [[def-csm-dk-hamiltonian-flow-measure]]. The finite-particle Hamiltonian, with energy in joules, is

$$H_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+\frac1N\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}W(q_i-q_j).$$

The interaction force is $K(q):=-\nabla_qW(q)$, in newtons. It is bounded and globally Lipschitz on the compact torus; evenness of $W$ makes $K$ odd and $K(0)=0$. Hamilton's equations in the canonical convention are

$$\dot q_i=\frac{p_i}{m},\qquad \dot p_i=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}K(q_i-q_j).$$

For any chosen momentum scale $P_0>0$ in kilogram-metres per second, define the time scale $\tau_0:=mL/P_0$ in seconds, dimensionless variables $x_i:=q_i/L\in\mathbb T^d:=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$, $v_i:=p_i/P_0$, and $s:=t/\tau_0$. Define the dimensionless potential $\Phi(x):=mW(Lx)/P_0^2$ and force $k(x):=-\nabla_x\Phi(x)$. Then the equations become

$$x_i'=v_i,\qquad v_i'=\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}k(x_i-x_j),$$

where prime denotes derivative with respect to dimensionless time $s$. Here
$\|Dk\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^d}\|Dk(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, with operator
norm induced by the Euclidean norm, and $\|k\|_\infty:=\sup_x|k(x)|$; the
constants $A:=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $B:=\|k\|_\infty$ are finite and
dimensionless. This is the selected smooth periodic mean-field scaling; it is
not the hard-sphere Boltzmann-Grad scaling.

Use the dimensionless one-particle phase space $Z:=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ from [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]], with its product topology and Borel sigma algebra. The finite torus is second-countable by [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]], and Euclidean space is second-countable. Consequently $Z$ and $Z\times Z$ are second-countable, and the Borel sigma algebra of each finite product equals the product of the factor Borel sigma algebras: every open set is a countable union of basic open rectangles. Use the product topology and its Borel sigma algebra on $Z\times Z$ as well.

For $x,y\in\mathbb T^d$, let

$$d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y):=\min_{\ell\in\mathbb Z^d}|\widetilde x-\widetilde y+\ell|,$$

where $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in\mathbb R^d$ are any representatives; the minimum is independent of the representatives. Equip $Z$ with

$$d_Z((x,v),(y,w)):=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)+|v-w|.$$

Let $\mathcal P_1(Z)$ be the Borel probability measures $\mu$ on $Z$ with $\int_Z|v|\,d\mu(x,v)<\infty$. For $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, a coupling is a Borel probability $\pi$ on $Z\times Z$ satisfying $\pi(A\times Z)=\mu(A)$ and $\pi(Z\times B)=\nu(B)$ for all Borel $A,B\subseteq Z$; write $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ for the set of couplings. Define the phase-space Wasserstein-1 coupling cost by

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{Z\times Z}d_Z(z,z')\,d\pi(z,z').$$

By [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], $\mu\otimes\nu$ is a probability on $\mathcal B(Z)\otimes\mathcal B(Z)=\mathcal B(Z\times Z)$ and its marginals are $\mu,\nu$; hence $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is nonempty. The infimum is finite: this product coupling has torus cost at most $\sqrt d/2$, and Tonelli's theorem bounds its velocity cost by $\int|v|\,d\mu+\int|w|\,d\nu$. No minimizing coupling is assumed to exist.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single

$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Thus $\eta$ is a nonnegative smooth probability density supported in the unit ball. For $0<\epsilon<1/4$, define $\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb R}(v)=\epsilon^{-d}\eta(v/\epsilon)$ and periodize it to $\mathbb T^d$ by $\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb T}(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\epsilon^{-d}\eta((\widetilde x+n)/\epsilon)$, where $\widetilde x$ is any representative. The sum is locally finite and independent of the representative; the fundamental-domain formula for $m_{\mathbb T^d}$ in [F5], followed by the change of variables $u=(\widetilde x+n)/\epsilon$, gives integral one, and its support satisfies $d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,0)\le\epsilon$. Differentiating the compactly supported smooth kernels under the integral shows that $f_\epsilon$ is smooth, and their nonnegativity and unit integrals give $\|f_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$. On their support, $d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)\le\epsilon$ and $|v-w|\le\epsilon$, so $\|f_\epsilon-f\|_\infty\le2\epsilon\operatorname{Lip}(f)$. u(C)$. The empty closed set has mass zero for both. Let $\mathcal D:=\{E\in\mathcal B(Z):\mu(E)=
u(E)\}$. Since $\mu$ and $

Apply [F4] to this pi-system and $\mathcal D$ to get $\mu=
u$.
